Cognac: Rémy Cointreau soars more than 10% in Paris as profits beat expectations despite Chinese and US tariffs

French cognac group Rémy Cointreau reported on Wednesday, November 25, a half-year operating profit of €126.7 million, up 16.6%, well above expectations. It raised its annual margin target. Its shares jumped more than 10%, the biggest gain in the SBF 120 [1][2][4].

From April to September 2026, current operating profit (what the normal business earns, before exceptional items) reached €126.7 million: +16.6% reported, +7.8% at constant exchange rates and scope (“organic”) [1]. The analysts' median was 116.6 million [2], and the consensus cited by Zonebourse expected only +4.3% organic growth [4].
Sales grew more slowly: €510.9 million, +2.9% organic and +4.4% reported thanks to currencies [2]. The operating margin rose from 22.2% to 24.8% [2].
Cognac carried the half-year: its margin climbed to 34.1% (+4.8 points), mainly thanks to a one-off cut in marketing, which will be ramped up again in the second half [7][3].

Net profit fell 9.8% to €57 million, weighed down by €25 million in exceptional items (restructuring, impairments) [2]. Recurring free cash flow rose back to €42 million, compared with −12.6 million a year earlier [2].
The group now targets a “solid” improvement in its margin for the fiscal year, instead of a “slight” increase [2]. Its CEO, Franck Marilly, spoke of “an encouraging turning point” [2].
On the stock market, the shares were up 10.5% at €56.80 around midday [4], then 12% at €57.50 around 4 p.m. [6], while the CAC 40 closed down 0.75% at 7,980.57 points [8].

The key takeaway: cognac is emerging from nearly three years of trade war with China. Beijing opened an investigation into European brandy in January 2024 [9], then imposed provisional duties in October, a “retaliatory measure” according to French minister Sophie Primas [10]. Since July 2025, Rémy Cointreau has been exempt by committing not to sell below a minimum price [11]. This agreement still weighs on its gross margin: around €5 million over the fiscal year [7].

On the United States side, the group recovered €6.4 million in customs duties paid last year [7]. Its Scotch whiskies and its Mount Gay rum, produced in the United Kingdom and Barbados, remain exempt from US tariffs [7].

Why such a jump? Investors compare the figures with their expectations, and profitability clearly beat the consensus: a “big beat” according to BFM Bourse [5]. The flip side: the shares are now worth 29.1 times expected earnings, more expensive than Pernod Ricard and Diageo according to Zonebourse [4].
A weakness remains: the margin also benefited from one-off marketing savings and currencies [3][7]. The second half will show whether the recovery holds.

If you have a PEA or a life insurance policy invested in French stocks, Rémy Cointreau is part of the SBF 120 [4]. Cognac, produced in Charente, is also a barometer of France's trade relations with Beijing and Washington: every tariff shows up immediately in the accounts. For the price of a bottle in France, nothing changes.

How it works: why the shares jump even though net profit falls

Rémy Cointreau's net profit fell 9.8% [2], and yet the shares soared. Investors look first at current operating profit, which measures what the normal business earns: it beat the analysts' median by €10 million (126.7 vs. 116.6 million) [2]. The drop in net profit comes from €25 million in exceptional charges, such as a restructuring [2]: one-time costs that should not recur. Above all, a stock reacts to the gap between the figures and expectations, and to the targets for what comes next. Here, the group raised its margin forecast [2]: analysts will revise up their estimates of future earnings, and the price adjusts during the same session.

For a group highly exposed to China, a political decision weighs more on the stock market than a quarter of sales.
Final decision: an average duty of 32.2% on European brandy [12], but Rémy Cointreau is exempt thanks to a minimum price commitment [11]. Its shares gain more than 20% in six sessions [13].
The stock market welcomes the end of uncertainty, even at the cost of slightly lower margins.

Egypt: Maersk tells Sisi of its full return to the Suez Canal, whose revenue doubled in November, and Norway's Scatec pledges $5 billion

On Wednesday, November 25, the head of Danish shipping giant Maersk told Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi that he wants to route all its services back through the Suez Canal and the Red Sea in the coming months. The same day, Norway's Scatec presented around $5 billion in investments over two years [1][2][3].

Maersk CEO Vincent Clerc explained that the group is working to bring all its lines back to Suez and the Red Sea over the coming months [1]. He also plans to load its ships more heavily and expand its fleet, meaning more Maersk vessels passing through the canal [1].
President Sisi assured that ships using the canal are safe and face no threat [1]. The chairman of the Suez Canal Authority hoped for a full return of shipping companies by March 2027 [1].
According to its chairman, Osama Rabie, the canal took in $593 million from November 1 to 24, 101.2% more than a year earlier ($295 million) [6].

Over the same period, 1,194 ships transited it, compared with 886 a year earlier, up 34.8%; net tonnage, which measures the volume carried, jumped 92.2% [6]. Already in October, revenue had climbed 94% year on year, to $724 million [7].

Scatec, a Norwegian renewable energy specialist, plans around $5 billion in new investments over two years [3]. On the agenda: seawater desalination powered by clean energy, “green” data centers, solar, wind, electricity storage and infrastructure [3][4].
The Egyptian president asked that more of the equipment be manufactured in Egypt [3]. That day he was receiving the heads of three international energy, water and transport groups [5].

The key takeaway: the Suez Canal, one of Egypt's main sources of foreign currency, is recovering. Its revenue already doubled in November with the return of several major shipping lines, and the announcement by Maersk, one of the world's container leaders, could bring others along [1][6].

Since the Red Sea crisis, attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels had pushed many shipowners to sail around Africa, a long detour. In October, traffic reached its highest monthly level since the start of this crisis [7]. Paradoxically, the war with Iran is now helping Suez: with the Strait of Hormuz almost closed, more ships are passing through the Egyptian canal, according to the specialist site Transport Topics [8].
The risk has not disappeared, however: the Houthis continue to threaten the southern Red Sea [8]. And the November figures cover only the first 24 days of the month [6].
Scatec's 5 billion adds to this good news for a country short of dollars [3][4].

Much of what you buy that is made in Asia reaches Europe by container. If ships return to the Suez route instead of sailing around Africa, the journey gets shorter, which can ease shipping costs and delivery times, provided the Red Sea stays safe.

Oil: drones over Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, and three more ships hit by mines in Hormuz according to Iran; Brent jumps 3.5%

On Wednesday, November 25, Saudi Arabia shot down four drones over Ras Tanura, its largest refinery, in an attack claimed by Yemen's Houthi rebels. The same day, Iran said two oil tankers and an LNG carrier had struck mines in Hormuz. Brent gained $3.21, to $94.61 [1][2][3][5].

The Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura on Wednesday morning. Debris fell, with no injuries according to an initial report, and it did not say whether the refinery had been hit [2].

The Houthis, allies of Iran, claim an attack in three waves against the refinery and against Riyadh's financial district. Their military spokesman, Yahya Saree, spoke of fires [3]. Satellite images from NASA and Planet Labs examined by Reuters show thick black smoke around the site [3]. Aramco did not respond [3].

In Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards say two oil tankers struck mines and caught fire early Wednesday, off the southern and eastern coasts of the strait, because they were using an “unauthorized” route [4][6]. Neither their names nor their flags were given [6].

On Wednesday evening, the Guards added that an LNG carrier, a ship that transports liquefied natural gas (LNG), had struck a mine after switching off its tracking system [5]. These claims could not be independently verified [4].
The Iranian military says it has installed new surveillance systems in the strait and warns that ships passing without coordinating with it are taking greater risks [4].

On the diplomatic front, Tehran repeats that it will not restore navigation until the US naval blockade of its ports is lifted and the war ends on all fronts. Through Qatari mediators, it offers to reopen the strait within 48 hours once these conditions are met [4].
Brent, the global oil benchmark, closed at $94.61 a barrel (+3.5%) and US WTI at $83.68 (+2%) [1]. In the morning, Brent was still falling, to $90.97 [7].

The key takeaway: what is new is the attack on a major Saudi oil facility, not just on ships. The market, which had reacted little to the mine announcements earlier in the day, this time sent Brent up 3.5% in a single session [1][7].

The Houthis have been firing at Saudi airports, oil sites and offices since the civil war in Yemen resumed in July, a spillover from the war between the United States and Iran [3]. Ras Tanura had already been targeted by two Iranian drones on March 2, 2026 [3].

Until now, expectations of a global oil surplus through 2027 had held prices back: Brent had started the day down 0.5% [4][7]. Wednesday's rise shows that this cushion offers poor protection against a direct attack on Gulf production [1].

Brent back near $95 means a tank of fuel that could cost a few cents more within one to two weeks. If attacks on Saudi sites continue, heating oil and heating gas could follow too, just as winter begins.

Jordan-Uzbekistan: in Amman, Mirziyoyev promises 40 projects worth $1.5 billion and signs 19 agreements, while trade between the two countries remains tiny

On Tuesday, November 24, in Amman, King Abdullah II of Jordan and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev raised their countries' relations to the level of a “strategic partnership”. Tashkent plans some forty investment projects in Jordan, worth around $1.5 billion, and is targeting $500 million in trade [1][2][4].

The Uzbek president announced around 40 investment projects in Jordan, worth close to $1.5 billion, according to the Jordan Times and Arab News [6][1]. It is not 15 billion, contrary to what the URL of the Arab News article suggests [1].
The two leaders signed an agreement establishing a strategic partnership and a joint declaration [2][3]. In total, 19 documents were signed during the visit [2].

These texts cover a preferential trade agreement (reduced customs duties between the two countries), energy, mining and geology, water, mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, culture, digital technology, health and pharmaceuticals, and urban planning [2].
The capitals Tashkent and Amman become twin cities, as do Samarkand and Petra, two historic sites popular with tourists [2].
The stated goal: raise trade to $500 million [2][5]. Arab News reports an increase of around 80% in trade since the king's last visit to Uzbekistan [1].
More than 20 companies with Jordanian capital already operate in Uzbekistan, according to the outlet Anewz [5]. The two leaders visited an exhibition of projects offered to investors [7].
To implement these agreements, the two countries plan to adopt a comprehensive “roadmap”, and Mirziyoyev invited the king to return to Uzbekistan [3].

The key takeaway: the announcement is ambitious, but the starting point is very low. Between 2017 and 2025, trade between the two countries rose from $850,000 to $8.53 million a year, according to Uzbek diplomacy [9]. Targeting 500 million means multiplying it by nearly 60.

The relationship has been accelerating since King Abdullah II's first state visit to Uzbekistan, in Samarkand, on August 25 and 26, 2025, which ended with 15 agreements [8]. It was then that the two countries launched preparations for the preferential trade agreement [10].

For Uzbekistan, a landlocked Central Asian country, Jordan offers a gateway to the Arab world. For Amman, which lacks capital, every foreign investor counts: the priority sectors cited range from transport to mining, including agriculture, textiles and pharmaceuticals [2].
The amounts announced remain intentions: no precise timetable has been published for these 40 projects, and their completion will depend on the promised roadmap [3][4].

For you, the direct effect is nil. But it is an example of an underlying trend: mid-sized countries, outside the orbit of the major powers, are forging trade ties with one another. Jordan, a neighbor of Israel, Syria and Iraq, is seeking to diversify its partners in a region at war.

2027 budget: the Senate reinstates the surtax on large companies that the deputies had scrapped, with €5 billion at stake

On Wednesday evening, November 25, the Senate voted by a show of hands to extend into 2027 the surtax on the profits of the largest groups, at a reduced rate. It is expected to bring in around €5 billion, compared with more than 7 billion in 2026. The deputies had scrapped it in late October, by just two votes [1][2][3].
The measure extends into 2027 the exceptional contribution on the profits of large companies, created by the 2025 finance law. It was adopted by a show of hands, at a lower rate than in 2026 [1].

The expected yield falls to around €5 billion in 2027, compared with an estimated 7.3 billion in 2026 [3][4]. Public Sénat describes a surtax “lightened by €2 billion”, passed without changes from the government's text [2].

On October 27, the National Assembly had scrapped this extension by 79 votes to 77 [4][5]. Then, on November 4, the deputies rejected the entire budget bill by 458 votes to 0, which sent it to the Senate in the government's version [6].
In the Senate, the review began on November 20. A motion to halt the debate was rejected by 249 votes to 19, with 77 abstentions [7].
Centrist Vincent Capo-Canellas believes that this surtax, supposed to be exceptional, has now become permanent. The left, on the contrary, wanted to increase it [2].
The Senate vote on the budget as a whole is scheduled for Wednesday, December 9 [8]. That will not be the end: the parliamentary calendar runs until December 17 [6].

The key takeaway: the €5 billion asked of large groups is back in the 2027 budget, after being struck out by the deputies. Without it, the state would have had to find this money elsewhere, or let its deficit slip [1][4].

A surtax is a tax added on top of the normal tax on profits (corporate income tax). It targets only the largest companies, those making the biggest profits in France. Created as a one- or two-year measure to plug holes in the budget, it is renewed year after year [1][2].

Public finances remain tight: the public deficit is around 5% of GDP and debt reached 119% of GDP at the end of June [9]. Every source of revenue counts, and the government can hardly do without 5 billion.

Nothing is final yet. The Senate's text will have to be reconciled with the Assembly, where the surtax had been narrowly rejected. The government could also resort to 49.3, the article of the Constitution that allows a text to be adopted without a vote, at the risk of a motion of no confidence [5].

If you are not a shareholder in a large group, this surtax does not affect you directly. But it is €5 billion that the state will not have to look for in other pockets, such as taxes on households or cuts to public services.

news.2026-11-26-afrique-du-sud-ramaphosa: South Africa: court sets aside the Phala Phala report, Ramaphosa escapes impeachment for now, opposition talks of appeal

On Wednesday, November 25, the Western Cape High Court set aside the report that paved the way for impeachment proceedings against President Cyril Ramaphosa, in the case of money stolen from his Phala Phala farm. The judges found that the panel of experts made “errors of law”. The opposition is considering an appeal [1][5][8].
Three judges [10] ruled the report unlawful and set it aside in its entirety, along with the steps taken by Parliament on that basis [8]. Each side will pay its own legal costs [8].

According to the court, the panel never reached the conclusion the rules required of it, and it went beyond the four charges Ramaphosa had to answer [6]. The judges also rejected the argument of former President Jacob Zuma's MK party that the court lacked jurisdiction [1].

The presiding judge, Justice Mabindla-Boqwana, specified that the Constitutional Court's ruling of May 2026 concerned the legality of Parliament's December 2022 vote, not how the panel had understood its mandate [1][8].
The judges warned that their decision does not mean the president should automatically escape parliamentary oversight [8]. Ramaphosa's conduct was not on trial, and the ruling does not clear him [4].
The presidency welcomed the decision. Its spokesman, Vincent Magwenya, said Ramaphosa had the right to challenge the report in court and that he will study the judgment [3].

ATM party leader Vuyo Zungula declared that “the courts are with Ramaphosa”; he will consult his lawyers and the other parties on an appeal, and believes Parliament can still appoint a new panel [5]. ActionSA promises to pursue “all possible avenues” [2].

The key takeaway: this is a major victory for Ramaphosa, which the business daily Business Day describes as his survival of “the biggest threat of his career” [4]. But the case is not closed: an appeal is expected and Parliament can restart proceedings [5][8].

The case dates back to the February 2020 burglary at the president's game farm, Phala Phala. A large sum in dollars, most often estimated at $580,000, was hidden there [9]. A panel chaired by former Chief Justice Sandile Ngcobo had concluded that there was prima facie evidence that Ramaphosa may have violated the Constitution and the law [9].

In December 2022, Parliament had refused to launch impeachment. On May 8, 2026, the Constitutional Court ruled that vote invalid and ordered the creation of a proper impeachment committee [7]. Ramaphosa then challenged the report itself, and in July obtained a suspension of the committee's work pending this judgment [6].
The debate now focuses on what comes next: the parliamentary impeachment committee is consulting Parliament's legal advisers, while the opposition is calling for a new panel [3][5].

The stability of South Africa, the continent's leading industrial economy, matters for the French companies based there and for emerging markets. An impeachment of the president would have opened a period of uncertainty; this judgment makes that less likely, without ruling it out entirely.

Mayors of France: presidential candidate David Lisnard re-elected with 72% of the vote, even better than in 2021

On Wednesday, November 25, at the 108th Mayors' Congress in Paris, David Lisnard, mayor of Cannes and candidate in the 2027 presidential election, was re-elected head of the Association of Mayors of France (AMF) with 72.06% of the vote. His rival Philippe Laurent accused him of using the association for his campaign [1][2].
David Lisnard won 9,505 votes, or 72.06%, against 3,686 votes (27.94%) for Philippe Laurent, UDI mayor of Sceaux (Hauts-de-Seine). Around 40% of the mayors eligible to vote took part [2].
Voting took place online from November 23 to 25, during the congress [7]. David Lisnard's lists also won the AMF's executive board and steering committee, with around 86% of the vote each [2].
In 2021, he had already beaten Philippe Laurent, with 62% of the vote against 38% [9]. Before the vote, he had gathered 106 endorsements, against 13 for his rival, with a required minimum of 11 [6].

Philippe Laurent criticized the outgoing president for using the AMF to raise his profile, even though the association says it is politically neutral [1]. David Lisnard promised to step back during the official presidential campaign, with a collegial leadership taking over at that point [1].

On the evening of the vote, he hailed “the mobilization of a grassroots France that no longer wants to have its destiny dictated to it” [3], and spoke of “the victory of an Association of Mayors of France that wants to remain independent” [4].
Former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe, also a declared presidential candidate, said he voted for him, calling him “a good president of the mayors” [4].

The congress, which opened on November 24 “against the backdrop of the battle for the Élysée”, according to Euronews, ends on Thursday afternoon, November 26, with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who is due to speak at a round table [5].

The key takeaway: despite criticism of his dual role, the mayors strengthened David Lisnard's position. He went from 62% in 2021 to 72% today [2][9], and enters the race for the Élysée with strong backing from mayors.

The AMF is the government's counterpart for all municipalities. It has a say on the money the state gives to towns, on the rules imposed on town halls and on the budget. This year, the 2027 budget bill was at the heart of the congress [8].

A declared presidential candidate remains at the head of an association that claims to be neutral. His rival saw this as a conflict of roles [1]. The mayors, for their part, seem above all to have rewarded a president who stands up to the state [3][4].

Turnout remains modest, around 40% [2]. But the margin is wide, and Édouard Philippe's support shows that the right and the center are treading carefully with a man who speaks on behalf of thousands of elected officials [4].

Your mayor depends partly on state money for schools, school canteens or roads. A strong AMF president who is also a presidential candidate can carry more weight in negotiations on the 2027 budget, and therefore on your municipality's services and, indirectly, on your property tax.

news.2026-11-26-allemagne-budget-2027-me: Germany: Merz defends the biggest budget in history, €560 billion, in the Bundestag; the opposition denounces a “debt orgy”

Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended the 2027 federal budget, of around €560 billion, the highest in the history of the Federal Republic, in the Bundestag on Wednesday, November 25. He called it “defensible”, while admitting that his coalition had struggled to finalize it [1][3]. The final vote is scheduled for Friday [4].
This budget alone adds around €210 billion in new debt next year, according to ZDF [1].
It calls for major savings over three years, especially in health [1].

The opposition is firing on all cylinders: for Tino Chrupalla (AfD), Merz is the “chancellor of insolvency”; Dietmar Bartsch (Die Linke) speaks of a “debt orgy”; Green MP Sebastian Schäfer of a “rickety shack without foundations” [2].

news.2026-11-26-inde-engins-chantier-pla: India: facing Chinese restrictions, Modi releases 11,000 crore rupees to build its own construction equipment

The Indian government approved on Wednesday, November 25, an 11,000 crore rupee plan (110 billion rupees) over eight years to push the country's factories to manufacture construction and infrastructure equipment, and their parts [1][2].
The plan runs for eight years, from fiscal year 2026-2027 to 2033-2034 [1].
Manufacturers of equipment and parts will receive a bonus on their additional sales for five years, starting at 13% and then tapering down to 8% [1].

The mechanism is simple: the more additional sales a factory makes, the more money the state pays it, with a bonus that decreases year after year to encourage it to quickly become competitive against foreign rivals [1].
